newsitem.title: USA: G7 warns against excessive currency volatility.
newsitem.headline: G7 warns against excessive currency volatility.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent

Major industrial nations warned against excessive volatility in currency markets on Sunday and stressed the importance of avoiding changes in exchange rates that could lead to lopsided trade relations.
Finance ministers and central bank chiefs from the Group of Seven richest countries emerged from a five-hour meeting generally upbeat about the outlook for their economies.
The G7 welcomed Russia's "imminent agreement" with the International Monetary Fund on a 1997 economic plan, but said Moscow should reform its tax system and deepen reforms.
In their communique, the G7 countries -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- said past misalignments of currency rates had been corrected, but challenges remained.

"We agreed that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility and significant deviations from fundamentals are undesirable," the G7 said. "We emphasised the importance of avoiding exchange rates that could lead to the reemergence of large external imbalances."

The comments seemed to reflect concern that a continued rise of the dollar, particularly against the Japanese yen, could lead to trade problems down the road. The dollar has risen more than 50 percent against the yen over the past two years, making Japanese exports more competitive.

German and Japanese officials made clear they opposed any further weakening of their currencies against the dollar, which reached a 4-1/2 year high against the yen and and a three-year peak against the German mark earlier this month.
Washington is worried that a weak yen will push Japan's trade surplus back up to troublesome levels.

Since the last G7 meeting in Berlin in February, the dollar has continued to climb on currency markets, helped by the strength of the U.S. economy and last month's U.S. quarter-point interest rate rise, while the yen and mark have suffered from the weakness of their domestic economies.
The G7 finance officials met during the biannual meeting of the IMF and World Bank.

The group said that its main aim remains balanced economic expansion and noted that many indicators in that regard were positive. Inflation is low and interest rates have generally declined over the past few years.
In an apprarent but not direct reference to Japan, the G7 said some member countries needed to continue to pay attention to ensuring the soundness of their financial systems.
Japan's banking system has been beset by huge amounts of bad loans, especially in the property market.
Japan has the objective of achieving strong domestic demand-led growth and avoiding a significant increase in its trade surplus, the G7 communique said.
The G7 said it also reviewed prospective monetary union in Europe and discussed what that meant for G7 economies. Europe is seeking to launch a single currency in 1999.
The group said it was worried Ukraine had not implemented an IMF reform agenda and they urged Kiev to go ahead "before further delays make the reform task more difficult."

The G7 said the 1997 deal between Russia and the IMF would act as a catalyst for private investment and for significant amounts of financing from the World Bank. "We welcome the expanded focus of this fund programme to include fiscal reforms for the long term and structural reforms," the statement said.

"We urge Russia to intensify its work with the World Bank to advance additional structural reforms. We look forward to an agreement that would permit Russia to participate in the Paris Club as a creditor on appropriate terms."
The G7 urged Russia to take "resolute action" to reform its tax policy and the tax system and to do more to encourage private investment.
"Deepened structural reform to improve the environment for private investment was seen as critical for propelling Russia onto a path of sustained growth" it said.
